title: Unconditional quantum advantage from a two-round CHSH problem in one dimension
authors: Yonghae Lee, Jeonghyeon Shin, Soojoon Lee
abstract: We introduce a relation problem constructed from the Clauser--Horne--Shimony--Holt (CHSH) game, which we call the two-round one-dimensional CHSH problem. Its two-round structure ensures that the CHSH questions are supplied only after the relevant Pauli-frame data have been fixed, thereby ruling out a simple classical strategy that solves the corresponding problem perfectly when all inputs are supplied simultaneously. We construct a quantum circuit on $2N$ qubits that uses only adjacent two-qubit gates, has operational depth at most eight, and achieves the optimal quantum success probability of CHSH, which is strictly smaller than one. We prove that, for every fixed $0\leqδ<(\sqrt{2}-1)/4$, any randomized classical circuit with fixed wiring and bounded gate fan-in that achieves an average success probability of at least $(2+\sqrt{2})/4-δ$ requires depth $Ω(\log N)$ after the questions of the second round are supplied. This yields an unconditional separation even though the quantum circuit is restricted to a one-dimensional geometry, whereas the classical circuit has no geometric locality restriction. The result shows that perfect quantum success is not necessary for unconditional quantum advantage with shallow circuits.
summary: This paper constructs a specific quantum game, the two-round 1D CHSH problem, to demonstrate an unconditional quantum advantage. It shows that a shallow quantum circuit can solve this problem optimally, while any classical circuit attempting to match this performance must exhibit super-polynomial circuit depth. This highlights that quantum advantage does not require perfect success probability or complex connectivity.
main_problem: The paper establishes an unconditional quantum advantage by analyzing a relation problem derived from the two-round CHSH game in one dimension (2R1D-CHSH).
main_result: It proves that the quantum circuit, restricted to a shallow depth and one dimension, achieves the optimal CHSH success probability, while any classical circuit achieving a comparable success probability requires super-polynomial depth ($\Omega(\log N)$).
method: The analysis compares the quantum success probability against the average success probability of randomized classical circuits, using techniques involving circuit depth bounding and temporal separation of inputs.
model_or_system: The model is the 2R1D-CHSH problem, implemented on a quantum circuit of $2N$ qubits using only adjacent two-qubit gates with a depth of at most eight.
key_observables: Quantum success probability ($\omega_q(	ext{CHSH}) = (2+\sqrt{2})/4$) and the required depth of the classical circuit ($\Omega(\log N)$).
important_parameters: The separation holds for any fixed $0 \le \delta < (\sqrt{2}-1)/4$. The size parameter is $N$.
main_assumptions: The quantum circuit is restricted to a one-dimensional geometry, and the classical circuit is assumed to have fixed wiring and bounded gate fan-in.
paper_structure: The paper defines the CHSH game and its generalization, formally defines the 2R1D-CHSH problem, constructs the shallow quantum circuit, bounds the classical performance, and finally combines these results to prove the depth separation.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, physically realizable example demonstrating quantum advantage using only local interactions (1D geometry) and shallow circuits, which is highly relevant for near-term quantum hardware.
